body_markdown:
All of the builds featured in our[Homegrown](https://www.hagerty.com/media/tags/homegrown/) series thus far have proudly waved the American flag. Take your seat for a notable exception: the just-completed Panache Art Deco coupé built by a father-and-son enterprise located 50 miles northwest of Toronto, Canada.


After retiring in 2007 from their successful logistics business, Dug Smith, now 64, and his father Garry, now 89, spent eight years re-educating themselves, followed by 10 years of effort designing and building their aptly named Panache.


My father studied tool and die technology, and I specialized in computer science,” says Dug. “This provided us with essential skills while revenue from our business funded the realization of our lifelong passion.


“My father completed his first cool car in 1957, a ’54 Mercury Meteor convertible with various custom touches which won second place at Toronto’s Rod and Custom show. His second project was a Ford Model A[channeled](https://www.hagerty.com/media/magazine-features/do-you-speak-hot-rodder-35-terms-for-high-powered-fluency/) six inches and powered by a Chevy V-8.


“We founded our current company,[Nasty Automobiles](https://www.nastyauto.com/) , in 2015 and began constructing Panache in 2019.


Dug Smith


“Three notable designs provided inspiration for our dream car: Bugatti’s Type 57, crafted and sold in low volume in the late-1930s; Chrysler’s 1995 Atlantic concept, created by Tom Gale and Bob Lutz; and the one-off Aquarius built in 2014 by James Hetfield, which is now on display at[the Petersen Museum](https://www.hagerty.com/media/tags/petersen-automotive-museum/) .


“We worked in our 3000-square-foot shop located at our home. Upon completion of our design on paper, a 3D print shop produced an electronic file to be used to create a full-sized physical buck. That file was turned over to a kitchen cabinet maker for the production of pressboard sections spaced six inches apart. Those pieces were assembled to create a ‘skeleton’ for shaping Panache’s aluminum body panels.


Dug Smith


“Our underpinnings began life as a 2012 Chevy Corvette powered by an LS3 6.2-liter V-8 rated at 430 horsepower and equipped with a 4L60E four-speed automatic. We stretched the Corvette’s frame 28 inches and bolstered its strength and stiffness with 2x4x3/8-inch tubing and 1/4-inch plate in key locations. Our final dimensions are: wheelbase, 129 inches; overall length, 207 inches; width, 81 inches; and height, 54 inches.


Dug Smith


“We used English wheels to shape our body panels. A total of three such tools were used—one purchased and two we built in our shop. All the work was done by our employee Dugald Cameron, my father, and myself. Father focused on smaller projects such as building the grille and taillights.


Dug Smith


“Our aim was to construct a rolling piece of art more reliable than any contemporary supercar. While practically all the fabrication occurred in-house, we did farm out the leather seat upholstery, the entertainment system, and some machining.


“Accents located throughout the car are carbon-fiber moldings created by us. The rear storage area accommodates two sets of golf clubs and several luggage cases. Stainless steel tubes built inside the doors serve two purposes: housing custom umbrellas and minimizing side-impact injury. Panache also contains a full, steel-tube rollcage for enhanced safety.


Dug Smith


“We constructed our head- and taillamp lenses of acrylic plastic. Panache’s polished cast-aluminum wheels were made in California by Savini. They’re fitted with Continental radial tires sized 285/45R-21 in front and 325/40R-22 in back.


nastyauto.com

“Thus far we’ve displayed Panache at two Canadian shows. We’ll show it soon at the Cobble Beach Concours on Lake Huron and at the Specialty Equipment Market Association (SEMA). Driving stints have been limited to our driveway and loading Panache for transport.


Dug Smith


“Our goal for the coming year is to provide the visibility Panache deserves before finding a suitable new owner for our pride and joy. In due course, Nasty Automobiles will move on to its next project. Our intention is to create our vision of moving art—versus commissioned work—to be shared with the world.”


Our bottom line: Art Deco never had it so good!
